item.title: Addressing Ultra-Low Fertility and Workforce Shrinkage: A Human-Centered HRM Response to the Demographic Crisis
item.content:encoded:
Ingyu Oh, Kansai Gaidai University

Jie Wu, University of Aberdeen

Ho Kwong Kwan, China Europe International Business School

Hyun Jeong Kim, Inha University

Low fertility is emerging as a critical challenge in international human resource management (HRM). Ultra-low fertility—defined as a total fertility rate (TFR) of 1.3 or lower—is no longer confined to East Asia. It is now present across diverse regions, including parts of Southern and Eastern Europe (e.g., Italy, Spain, Poland), high-income Asian economies (e.g., South Korea, Japan, Singapore), and is increasingly affecting advanced economies in North America and Oceania. As of 2022, around 20 countries face ultra-low fertility, while 152 nations fall below the replacement level of 2.1.

This demographic crisis is transforming HRM from a support function into a strategic imperative. Policymakers around the world are sounding the alarm—South Korea warns of 'national extinction,' Japan calls it a 'quiet emergency,' and several European nations are grappling with labor market stagnation. The risks of shrinking workforces, declining productivity, and rising costs for talent acquisition and retention are now central economic concerns.

Appel publié par The International Journal of Human Resource Management. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Work-Life Balance Challenges: Family-friendly HRM policies and workplace cultures affecting fertility decisions
  • Work-Life Balance Challenges: Gender inequality, maternity/paternity leave, and childcare support impacts on career and family planning
  • Work-Life Balance Challenges: Cultural expectations and traditional gender roles influencing fertility rates
  • Work-Life Balance Challenges: Implementing on-site childcare, generous parental leave, and financial incentives for families
  • Work-Life Balance Challenges: Fostering inclusive environments prioritizing work-life balance and psychological safety
  • Adapting HR Practices: Flexible work policies including remote work, reduced hours, and enhanced parental leave
  • Adapting HR Practices: Upskilling and reskilling programs addressing workforce shrinkage
  • Adapting HR Practices: Inclusive benefits such as childcare support, eldercare programs, and fertility treatments
  • Adapting HR Practices: Diversity and inclusion strategies tapping underutilized labor pools (older workers, women, immigrants)
  • Adapting HR Practices: Innovative international recruitment strategies and talent pipeline development
  • Human-Centered AI Solutions: Deploying AI tools enhancing productivity without undermining employee wellbeing or autonomy
  • Human-Centered AI Solutions: AI-assisted work-life balance through predictive analytics and personalized leave planning
  • Human-Centered AI Solutions: AI-facilitated servant leadership and psychological safety reducing family planning fears
  • Human-Centered AI Solutions: AI-driven personalized work schedules for dual-earner couples
  • Human-Centered AI Solutions: Digital twin modeling simulating and optimizing career-family pathways
  • Human-Centered AI Solutions: AI and automation addressing labor shortages and optimizing workforce management
  • Rethinking Core HRM Theories: Developing scarcity-based view and demographic agility in HRM
  • Rethinking Core HRM Theories: Human capital preservation and the demographic premium concept
  • Institutional and Cultural Complexity: Reconciling global HR best practices with local fertility norms
  • Institutional and Cultural Complexity: Institutional fertility regimes and institutional entrepreneurship in gender-equity reforms
  • Institutional and Cultural Complexity: Cultural paradoxes and the influence of cultural tightness-looseness on policy uptake
